front: What are the three practical breast cancer groups by receptor status, and what is the systemic backbone of each?
back: HR+/HER2-: endocrine therapy. HER2+: HER2-directed therapy (trastuzumab ± pertuzumab) with chemo. Triple-negative: chemo, often with immunotherapy.
extra: HR+/HER2- is the most common and often relatively indolent; triple-negative is often more aggressive and more common in younger patients and BRCA1 carriers. The luminal/basal-like names map roughly onto these groups. Endocrine therapy is usually tamoxifen before menopause and an aromatase inhibitor after.

front: Which breast cancer subtypes respond best to neoadjuvant chemotherapy?
back: HER2-positive and triple-negative (the more aggressive subtypes)
extra: The paradox: a high pathologic complete response rate does not mean the best long-term prognosis. HR+/HER2- tumors respond least.

front: Which germline findings should make a radiation oncologist pause before treating, and which one should not?
back: Pause: Li-Fraumeni (TP53), because of radiation-induced second cancers, and homozygous ATM (ataxia-telangiectasia), because of severe radiosensitivity. BRCA1/2 alone does not contraindicate RT.
extra: In Li-Fraumeni, mastectomy is often chosen so radiation can be avoided when a reasonable alternative exists. Heterozygous ATM carriers are not automatically unsafe to treat. A BRCA result feeds into the lumpectomy vs mastectomy discussion with genetic counseling.

front: What common thread links most breast cancer risk factors?
back: More lifetime estrogen exposure (early menarche, late menopause, nulliparity or late first birth, HRT, postmenopausal obesity)
extra: Other risks: prior DCIS, LCIS, or atypia; dense breasts; family history; and chest radiation at a young age (e.g., Hodgkin mantle field).

front: How do DCIS and LCIS differ in what they mean and how they are treated?
back: DCIS is a true precursor and is treated (surgery ± RT). LCIS is mainly a risk marker and is not treated with RT.
extra: LCIS is no longer staged as Tis. Both ductal and lobular cancers start in the terminal duct lobular unit.

front: What protein is lost in invasive lobular carcinoma, and why is ILC hard to see on a mammogram?
back: E-cadherin. Without it, cells spread in single-file lines instead of forming a mass, so mammography underestimates ILC and MRI is often used to define its extent.
extra: ILC is more often multicentric or bilateral, almost always ER+/HER2-, lower grade, and less FDG-avid.

front: Which breast cancer subtype is linked to BRCA1, and which features does BRCA2 cancer tend to have?
back: BRCA1: triple-negative cancer. BRCA2: cancer that looks more like sporadic HR+ disease, and a higher risk of male breast cancer.
extra: Neither gene alone makes radiation unsafe. The result belongs in the shared decision about lumpectomy plus RT vs mastectomy.

front: Why do women treated with mantle-field radiation for Hodgkin lymphoma get high-risk breast screening?
back: Chest radiation at a young age substantially raises breast cancer risk.
extra: High-risk screening adds breast MRI. Prior chest radiation also makes breast-conserving radiation harder or impossible later.

front: Where does invasive lobular carcinoma metastasize that ductal cancer usually does not?
back: Unusual sites: the peritoneum, GI tract, ovaries, and meninges
extra: ILC is almost always HR+/HER2-, lower grade, and less FDG-avid, so PET can miss it.

front: Which breast tumors are most likely to drain to the internal mammary nodes, and why does covering them matter for RT?
back: Medial and central tumors. Covering the internal mammary nodes raises heart and lung dose, especially on the left.
extra: Most lymph (about 75%) goes to the axilla from every quadrant. The upper outer quadrant has the most cancers.

front: How does the pectoralis minor define axillary levels I, II, and III?
back: Level I is lateral to it, level II is behind it, and level III (infraclavicular) is medial to it.
extra: The pectoralis minor is the whole answer. Sentinel nodes are usually in level I.

front: A standard axillary dissection removes which levels, and what does regional nodal irradiation add?
back: Levels I and II. Regional nodal RT covers level III (infraclavicular), the supraclavicular nodes, and usually the internal mammary nodes, plus any undissected axilla at risk.
extra: The brachial plexus sits behind the supraclavicular and level III targets, so high nodal doses risk plexopathy.

front: Which breast quadrant has the most cancers, and why?
back: The upper outer quadrant (about half of cancers), because it has the most glandular tissue
extra: It includes the axillary tail of Spence. The lower inner quadrant has the fewest cancers.

front: Does skin dimpling make a breast cancer T4? Does invasion of the pectoralis muscle alone?
back: No to both. Dimpling is the tumor pulling on Cooper's ligaments, and pectoralis invasion alone is not chest wall invasion.
extra: T4a requires chest wall invasion (ribs, intercostals, serratus). T4b requires ulceration, satellite skin nodules, or peau d'orange.

front: Where are the internal mammary nodes, and why does treating them matter on a left-sided plan?
back: Next to the sternum in intercostal spaces 1-3. Including them brings the field close to the heart and raises heart dose.
extra: Medial and central tumors are most likely to drain there.

front: A breast cancer patient has a positive contralateral axillary node. Is that N3 or M1?
back: M1. Contralateral nodes count as distant metastasis.
extra: Ipsilateral supraclavicular, infraclavicular, and internal mammary nodes are regional (N2-N3) and still curable.

front: Which BI-RADS categories mean the lesion should be biopsied?
back: BI-RADS 4 (suspicious) and 5 (highly suggestive of cancer)
extra: BI-RADS 3 (probably benign) gets short-interval follow-up; BI-RADS 6 is already biopsy-proven cancer. Suspicious mammogram findings: spiculated mass, pleomorphic or linear-branching calcifications, architectural distortion.

front: When is breast MRI used?
back: High-risk screening, defining extent of disease (especially lobular cancer), and judging response to neoadjuvant chemo
extra: It is the most sensitive breast test but only moderately specific, so routine MRI adds biopsies and mastectomies without improving survival.

front: On the breast planning CT, what defines the tumor bed for a boost or partial breast treatment?
back: The lumpectomy cavity (seroma) and the surgical clips
extra: Simulation is done in the treatment position, usually on a breast board with arms up.

front: For left-sided breast RT, what technique lowers heart dose, and how does it work?
back: Deep inspiration breath hold (DIBH): a deep breath moves the heart away from the chest wall and out of the tangent fields.
extra: Darby: major cardiac events rise about 7% per Gy of mean heart dose.

front: Which three mammogram findings are suspicious for cancer?
back: A spiculated mass, pleomorphic or linear-branching calcifications, and architectural distortion
extra: Calcifications alone are the classic way DCIS shows up, and linear branching calcifications suggest higher-grade DCIS.

front: What does BI-RADS 3 mean, and what is the next step?
back: Probably benign (2% or less cancer risk). Short-interval follow-up imaging in about 6 months, not biopsy.
extra: BI-RADS 0 means incomplete (more imaging needed), and BI-RADS 6 means biopsy-proven cancer.

front: What ultrasound features make an axillary lymph node suspicious?
back: A thickened cortex and loss of the fatty hilum
extra: A suspicious node gets an ultrasound-guided biopsy and a clip.

front: Why is a clip placed in a biopsy-proven positive axillary node before neoadjuvant therapy?
back: So the node can be found and removed at surgery even if it shrinks and is no longer visible
extra: Targeted axillary surgery after a good response depends on removing the clipped node.

front: Why is breast MRI not ordered for every newly diagnosed breast cancer?
back: It is very sensitive but only moderately specific. Routine use leads to extra biopsies and more mastectomies without improving survival.
extra: It is used when the answer changes management: high-risk screening, extent (especially ILC), response to neoadjuvant therapy, and an occult primary.

front: How much does the risk of major cardiac events rise with mean heart dose in breast radiation?
back: Roughly 7% per Gy of mean heart dose (Darby)
extra: This linear relationship is why left-sided plans work hard to lower heart dose, often with deep inspiration breath hold.

front: Why is a core needle biopsy preferred over FNA for a breast lesion?
back: FNA gives cells without tissue architecture, so it cannot tell DCIS from invasive cancer; a core biopsy can.
extra: A clip is placed at biopsy so the site can be found later, which matters after neoadjuvant chemo.

front: Which breast cancer patients need systemic staging imaging (CT chest/abdomen/pelvis + bone scan, or PET/CT)?
back: Higher-risk or locally advanced disease (e.g., clinical stage III: T4, N2-3, inflammatory), or anyone whose symptoms, exam, or labs suggest metastasis
extra: Often considered for some stage II patients going to neoadjuvant therapy; it is not a strict stage-number rule. Brain MRI only for symptoms. In asymptomatic early-stage disease, body imaging finds more false positives than metastases. PET is good at finding hidden internal mammary, infraclavicular, and supraclavicular nodes.

front: What counts as a negative margin after lumpectomy for invasive cancer vs DCIS?
back: Invasive cancer: no tumor on ink. DCIS: at least 2 mm.
extra: DCIS needs a wider margin because calcifications underestimate its true extent.

front: What are the breast cancer T-stage size cutoffs, and what makes a tumor T4 regardless of size?
back: T1 ≤2 cm, T2 >2-5 cm, T3 >5 cm. T4 = chest wall invasion or skin involvement (ulceration, satellite nodules, peau d'orange) or inflammatory cancer.
extra: Traps: skin dimpling alone is not T4, and invasion of the pectoralis muscle alone is not chest wall invasion.

front: How is inflammatory breast cancer diagnosed, and what T stage is it?
back: Clinically: rapid-onset erythema and edema of at least 1/3 of the breast, confirmed with a skin biopsy. It is T4d.
extra: Often there is no discrete mass. It is at least stage IIIB.

front: A 1.5 cm breast cancer has a biopsy-proven ipsilateral supraclavicular node. What is the stage, and is the goal still cure?
back: cN3c, stage IIIC. Yes: supraclavicular nodes are regional, not distant, so she is treated for cure (neoadjuvant systemic therapy, surgery, and comprehensive nodal RT including the supraclavicular fossa).
extra: Any N3 is stage IIIC no matter how small the primary is. A contralateral axillary or supraclavicular node, by contrast, is M1.

front: What separates clinical N1, N2, and N3 in breast cancer?
back: N1 = movable level I/II axillary nodes. N2 = fixed/matted axillary nodes, or internal mammary nodes alone. N3 = infraclavicular, internal mammary plus axillary, or supraclavicular nodes.
extra: Breast N stage depends on which basin is involved as much as how many nodes.

front: Which pathologic axillary node counts separate pN1, pN2, and pN3?
back: 1-3 nodes = pN1, 4-9 = pN2, 10 or more = pN3
extra: These are the counts that drive post-mastectomy radiation decisions.

front: What is the difference between anatomic and prognostic stage in breast cancer, and which one do radiation fields follow?
back: Anatomic = T + N + M (where the cancer is). Prognostic = anatomic plus grade, ER, PR, HER2 ± genomic score (how biology changes outlook). Fields follow the anatomic extent, not prognostic stage alone.
extra: Favorable biology can lower the prognostic stage and triple-negative disease often raises it, but a node-positive patient downstaged by biology still has node-positive disease for RT planning.

front: How is a breast lesion seen only as calcifications biopsied?
back: Stereotactic (mammogram-guided) core biopsy
extra: Masses are usually biopsied with ultrasound guidance, MRI-only lesions with MRI guidance, and suspected inflammatory or Paget disease with a skin punch biopsy.

front: Is LCIS staged as Tis? Which lesions are?
back: No. LCIS is no longer staged as cancer. Tis is DCIS, or Paget disease of the nipple without an underlying tumor.
extra: LCIS is a risk marker for both breasts and is not treated with radiation.

front: How is a sentinel node with only isolated tumor cells (0.2 mm or smaller) staged?
back: pN0(i+): it still counts as node-negative.
extra: Micrometastasis (more than 0.2 mm to 2 mm) is pN1mi.

front: What does ypT0 ypN0 mean after neoadjuvant therapy?
back: Pathologic complete response (pCR): no invasive cancer left in the breast or the nodes at surgery
extra: A pCR is a strong prognostic sign, but it does not erase the pre-treatment clinical stage for the radiation decision.

front: Which way does biology push the AJCC prognostic stage in breast cancer?
back: Favorable biology (ER+/PR+/HER2+ or low-grade ER+) often lowers the stage. Triple-negative or high-grade disease often raises it.
extra: You do not need to memorize the prognostic table. Radiation fields still follow the anatomic extent.

front: Which breast cancer patients should be offered genetic counseling and testing?
back: Those with young age at diagnosis, triple-negative cancer, a strong family history, Ashkenazi Jewish ancestry, or male breast cancer
extra: A germline result can change the choice between breast conservation and mastectomy.

front: How does survival with lumpectomy plus radiation compare with mastectomy?
back: It is the same (NSABP B-06, Milan).
extra: Radiation is part of the breast-conserving package: it roughly halves recurrence after lumpectomy (EBCTCG).

front: Which patient factors can make breast radiation (and so lumpectomy) unsafe?
back: Pregnancy (RT cannot be given during it) and prior radiation to the breast/chest; relative ones are active scleroderma or lupus and Li-Fraumeni syndrome.
extra: Tumor factors against lumpectomy: inflammatory cancer, diffuse suspicious calcifications, persistently positive margins.

front: What does radiation after lumpectomy for DCIS accomplish, and when can it be skipped?
back: It halves in-breast recurrence (about half of recurrences are invasive) without changing survival. It can be omitted for low-risk DCIS (small, low/intermediate grade, widely clear margins).
extra: DCIS treated with mastectomy needs no RT.

front: What are the standard hypofractionated whole-breast radiation regimens?
back: 40 Gy in 15 fractions (3 weeks) or 26 Gy in 5 fractions (1 week)
extra: START B and FAST-Forward showed these match longer courses for control and side effects.

front: Which features call for a tumor bed boost after whole-breast RT?
back: Younger age (about ≤50), high grade, or a close/positive margin that cannot be re-excised
extra: Typical boost: 10 Gy in 4 fractions, or a simultaneous boost.

front: Which patients can reasonably omit radiation after lumpectomy for invasive cancer?
back: Older patients (about ≥65-70) with small (T1), node-negative, ER+ tumors, clear margins, who take endocrine therapy
extra: CALGB 9343 and PRIME II: skipping RT raised local recurrence slightly with no survival difference. Partial breast RT is another option for low-risk patients.

front: What did ACOSOG Z0011 show?
back: For cT1-2 cN0 patients with 1-2 positive sentinel nodes treated with lumpectomy and whole-breast RT, skipping axillary dissection did not change survival.
extra: AMAROS: for a positive sentinel node, axillary RT instead of dissection gave the same control with about half the lymphedema. Tangent fields already dose part of axillary level I (more with "high tangents"), part of why skipping dissection worked.

front: What does radiation add once breast cancer is node-positive, and what is the evidence?
back: Regional nodal irradiation (level III, supraclavicular, and internal mammary nodes) on top of the breast or chest wall; MA.20 and EORTC 22922 showed better disease-free survival.
extra: Four or more positive nodes almost always get RNI; 1-3 nodes usually do, weighed with tumor biology, location, and the axillary surgery done.

front: Why is a dissected axilla (levels I-II) usually not retreated with radiation?
back: Radiation on top of an axillary dissection sharply raises lymphedema risk.
extra: Axillary dissection alone causes lymphedema in about 20-25% of patients, which is why sentinel node biopsy is standard for a clinically negative axilla.

front: After neoadjuvant therapy, which stage do you use for the radiation decision?
back: Both: the pre-treatment clinical stage (cT/cN) and the post-surgery response (ypT/ypN), plus the biology. A complete response does not erase the original stage.
extra: Locally advanced disease (e.g., cN3c) still gets comprehensive nodal RT after a pCR. For cN1 that converts to ypN0, NSABP B-51 found no significant benefit from adding regional nodal RT, so omission can be discussed. Always record the pre-treatment cT and cN.

front: What are the clear indications for post-mastectomy radiation (PMRT)?
back: 4 or more positive nodes, T4 disease (or T3 with positive nodes), or a positive margin
extra: Strongly considered for 1-3 positive nodes; T3N0 is individualized. PMRT treats the chest wall plus regional nodes, with bolus when the skin is at risk.

front: What surgery and radiation does inflammatory breast cancer get after neoadjuvant chemo?
back: Modified radical mastectomy (no lumpectomy, no sentinel node biopsy), then PMRT to the chest wall with bolus plus all regional nodes
extra: Reconstruction is delayed.

front: How is chemotherapy sequenced with breast radiation?
back: Generally not at the same time: cytotoxic chemo is given before surgery or after surgery but before RT.
extra: Concurrent chemo with breast RT adds skin and other toxicity. Anti-HER2 drugs and endocrine therapy can continue during RT; endocrine therapy then runs for years.

front: What is the most common acute side effect of breast radiation, and where is it usually worst?
back: Radiation dermatitis (redness, itching, peeling), worst in skin folds such as the inframammary fold and axilla
extra: Builds over the course and peaks around the end of treatment; fatigue is also common. Bolus and large breasts make it worse. Moist desquamation is a more severe grade.

front: What are the main organs at risk in breast and regional nodal radiation?
back: The heart (especially the LAD on the left) and the ipsilateral lung; with nodal fields, also the brachial plexus.
extra: Medial tumors and internal mammary coverage raise heart and lung dose. Late effects: cardiac events, pneumonitis, plexopathy (rare), and lymphedema when the axilla is treated after dissection.

front: Does meeting Z0011 criteria (1-2 positive sentinel nodes, no axillary dissection) mean the patient gets no regional nodal RT?
back: No. Z0011 answers the surgical question (skip ALND). Whether to treat the regional nodes is a separate decision based on nodal burden, biology, location, and other risk features.
extra: Z0011 patients were treated with whole-breast tangents, often high tangents. MA.20 and EORTC 22922 are the trials behind adding regional nodal RT.

front: What did the EBCTCG meta-analysis show about radiation after lumpectomy?
back: It halved recurrence and prevented about 1 breast cancer death for every 4 recurrences prevented.
extra: After mastectomy for node-positive disease, radiation also lowered recurrence and breast cancer mortality.

front: What did AMAROS show for a positive sentinel node?
back: Axillary radiation instead of axillary dissection gave the same axillary control with about half the lymphedema.
extra: Axillary dissection causes lymphedema in about 20-25% of patients.

front: Does a patient who has a mastectomy for DCIS need radiation?
back: No. Mastectomy for DCIS needs no radiation.
extra: After lumpectomy for DCIS, radiation roughly halves in-breast recurrence (NSABP B-17, EORTC 10853), with no survival difference.

front: Which patients are candidates for partial breast irradiation?
back: Low-risk patients (generally 40 or older) with small (≤2 cm), node-negative, ER+, lower-grade tumors and clear margins
extra: Representative regimens are 30 Gy in 5 fractions or 40 Gy in 15 fractions to the tumor bed only.

front: Which trials established hypofractionated and then 1-week whole-breast radiation?
back: START B (40 Gy in 15 fractions) and FAST-Forward (26 Gy in 5 fractions)
extra: Both matched longer courses for local control and side effects, so hypofractionation is now standard for whole-breast RT.

front: What did the EORTC 22881 boost trial show?
back: A 16 Gy tumor bed boost after whole-breast RT lowered local recurrence, with the largest absolute benefit in younger patients and no survival difference.
extra: The cost of a boost is more fibrosis and a slightly worse cosmetic result.

front: Which systemic therapies can safely run during breast radiation, and which cannot?
back: Anti-HER2 antibodies (such as trastuzumab) and endocrine therapy can run during RT. Cytotoxic chemotherapy is not given at the same time.
extra: The usual order is surgery, adjuvant chemotherapy if needed, radiation, then years of endocrine therapy.

front: What did KEYNOTE-522 add for stage II-III triple-negative breast cancer?
back: Pembrolizumab with neoadjuvant chemotherapy (continued after surgery) raised the pCR rate and improved event-free survival.
extra: Residual triple-negative disease after neoadjuvant therapy gets capecitabine, or olaparib if germline BRCA.

front: What is given after surgery for HER2-positive breast cancer with residual disease after neoadjuvant therapy?
back: T-DM1 (KATHERINE)
extra: Neoadjuvant chemotherapy plus anti-HER2 therapy produces a high pCR rate in HER2-positive disease.

front: What question did NSABP B-51 ask, and what did it find?
back: Whether biopsy-proven cN1 patients whose nodes became ypN0 after neoadjuvant chemo need regional nodal RT. Adding it did not significantly reduce invasive recurrence.
extra: Omitting nodal RT in this group is now a reasonable discussion, not a rule. B-51 does not apply to cN2-N3 disease.

front: A cN3c breast cancer has a complete response to neoadjuvant therapy. Can comprehensive nodal radiation be skipped?
back: No. For locally advanced disease, radiation follows the pre-treatment stage, so comprehensive RT (including the supraclavicular fossa) is given even after a pCR.
extra: Locally advanced includes T4, inflammatory, and N2-N3 disease.

front: Why does the radiation oncologist need to be involved in planning breast reconstruction?
back: Radiation raises implant and reconstruction complications.
extra: For inflammatory breast cancer, reconstruction is usually delayed until after PMRT.
